subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: Parliament legislates on banking through Entry 45 of the Union List. Which of the following is excluded from the Banking Regulation Act, 1949?

options.A: A primary agricultural credit society and a cooperative land mortgage bank
options.B: A banking company incorporated outside India carrying on business in India
options.C: A local area bank licensed by the Reserve Bank of India to carry on business
options.D: A banking company which has been prohibited from receiving fresh deposits

answer_html:
Answer: (A) A primary agricultural credit society and a cooperative land mortgage bank.

The Banking Regulation Act, 1949 is a central legislation that regulates all banking firms in India, and Parliament has the power to legislate on banking through Entry 45 of the Union List. Primary agricultural credit societies and cooperative land mortgage banks are excluded from the Act. The Act gives the Reserve Bank power to license banks, to regulate shareholding and voting rights, to supervise the appointment of boards and management, to lay down instructions for audits, to impose moratorium, mergers and liquidation, and to impose penalties.
topic_text: Scope of the Banking Regulation Act

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: Section 15 prohibits a banking company from paying any dividend on its shares until-

options.A: it has completely written off all its capitalized expenses
options.B: it has transferred one half of its profit to the reserve fund
options.C: it has obtained the previous approval of the Central Government
options.D: it has completed five years from the grant of its banking licence

answer_html:
Answer: (A) it has completely written off all its capitalized expenses.

Section 15 prohibits every banking company from paying any dividend on its shares unless it has completely written off its capitalized expenses, such as preliminary expenses and brokerage and commission on the issue of shares. A dividend may nevertheless be paid without writing off depreciation in the value of investments in approved securities not actually capitalized or accounted for as a loss, depreciation in other investments where adequate provision approved by the auditor has been made, and bad debts adequately provided for.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: Every banking company must ensure that its Board of Directors consists of persons having specialised knowledge or practical experience in the specified fields to the extent of-

options.A: the whole of the Board, no person without specialised knowledge or practical experience being eligible for appointment as a director at all
options.B: not less than 51% of the total number of directors, of whom a minimum of two must have such knowledge in agriculture and rural economy, co-operation and small scale industry
options.C: not less than 51% of the total number of directors, of whom a minimum of two must be nominees of the Reserve Bank of India appointed for the purpose
options.D: not less than one third of the total number of directors, of whom a minimum of two must have such knowledge in agriculture and rural economy alone

answer_html:
Answer: (B) not less than 51% of the total number of directors, of whom a minimum of two must have such knowledge in agriculture and rural economy, co-operation and small scale industry.

Not less than 51% of the total number of the Board of Directors must consist of persons having specialised knowledge or practical experience in accountancy, agriculture and rural economy, banking, co-operation, finance, law, small scale industry or any other field which in the opinion of the Reserve Bank would be useful, and there shall be a minimum of two persons with special knowledge or experience in agriculture and rural economy, co-operation and small scale industry. The Reserve Bank may order the reconstitution of the Board of any bank.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: Under Section 12 the capital structure of a banking company must be such that-

options.A: the paid-up capital is not less than half of the authorised capital and the subscribed capital is not less than half of the paid-up capital
options.B: the subscribed capital and the paid-up capital are each not less than one fourth of the authorised capital of the company
options.C: the subscribed capital is not less than half of the authorised capital and the paid-up capital is not less than half of the subscribed capital
options.D: the subscribed capital is not less than the whole of the authorised capital and the paid-up capital not less than half of it

answer_html:
Answer: (C) the subscribed capital is not less than half of the authorised capital and the paid-up capital is not less than half of the subscribed capital.

Section 12 requires that the subscribed capital of the company be not less than half of its authorised capital and the paid-up capital not less than half of its subscribed capital. Where the authorised capital is increased, that proportion may be permitted to be secured within a period not exceeding two years from the date of the increase, or as per Reserve Bank guidelines. The shares may be equity or preference shares.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: Section 17 obliges a banking company to transfer to its reserve fund a sum equivalent to not less than 20% of the profit each year. The Reserve Bank has separately directed that all scheduled commercial banks operating in India, including foreign banks, transfer to the reserve fund not less than-

options.A: 50% of the net profit before appropriations
options.B: 25% of the net profit before appropriations
options.C: 20% of the net profit before appropriations
options.D: 10% of the net profit before appropriations

answer_html:
Answer: (B) 25% of the net profit before appropriations.

The statutory minimum under Section 17 is a transfer of not less than 20% of the profit each year to the reserve fund, and that obligation does not apply where the amount in the reserve fund together with the share premium account is more than or equal to the paid-up capital, exemption being granted by the Central Government on the recommendation of the Reserve Bank. Separately, all scheduled commercial banks operating in India including foreign banks should transfer not less than 25 per cent of the net profit before appropriations to the reserve fund. Any appropriation of reserves must be intimated to the Reserve Bank within 21 days with reasons.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: The return of unclaimed deposits under Section 26 relates to accounts which have not been operated in India for-

options.A: 10 years, and must be submitted within 30 days after the close of each financial year
options.B: 5 years, and must be submitted within 60 days after the close of each calendar year
options.C: 7 years, and must be submitted within 30 days after the close of each calendar year
options.D: 10 years, and must be submitted within 30 days after the close of each calendar year

answer_html:
Answer: (D) 10 years, and must be submitted within 30 days after the close of each calendar year.

The return gives particulars of accounts un-operated in India for 10 years and is to be submitted within 30 days after the close of each calendar year. In the case of a fixed deposit the period of 10 years is counted from the date of expiry of the fixed period. Regional rural banks forward such returns to the National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development rather than to the Reserve Bank.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: Under Section 24 a banking company must maintain liquid assets of a percentage of its total time and demand liabilities not exceeding 40%, computed as on the last Friday of the second preceding fortnight. Those liquid assets-

options.A: comprise cash, gold or unencumbered approved securities valued at a price not exceeding the current market price
options.B: comprise cash and balances with the Reserve Bank alone, gold and securities being expressly excluded from the account
options.C: comprise any assets held in India, valued at the price at which they were acquired by the banking company
options.D: comprise cash, gold or unencumbered approved securities valued at their face value irrespective of market price

answer_html:
Answer: (A) comprise cash, gold or unencumbered approved securities valued at a price not exceeding the current market price.

The liquid assets for the purposes of Section 24 include cash, gold or unencumbered approved securities, and they are valued at a price not exceeding the current market price. The percentage is specified by the Reserve Bank by notification in the Official Gazette and cannot exceed 40% of the total of time and demand liabilities, reckoned as on the last Friday of the second preceding fortnight. Separately, Section 25 requires the maintenance of assets equivalent to at least 75% of demand and time liabilities in India, at the close of business on the last Friday of every quarter.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: Where a banking company is temporarily unable to meet its obligations, it may apply for an order staying the commencement or continuance of all legal actions and proceedings against it. Such an application-

options.A: is made to the High Court, the stay may not exceed 6 months, and it must be accompanied by a report of the Reserve Bank that the company will be able to pay its debts
options.B: is made to the Reserve Bank, the stay may not exceed 6 months, and it must be accompanied by a report of the auditor that the company will be able to pay its debts
options.C: is made to the High Court, the stay may not exceed 12 months, and no report of the Reserve Bank is required where the company is a scheduled bank
options.D: is made to the Central Government, the stay may not exceed 3 months, and it must be accompanied by a resolution of the Board of Directors of the company

answer_html:
Answer: (A) is made to the High Court, the stay may not exceed 6 months, and it must be accompanied by a report of the Reserve Bank that the company will be able to pay its debts.

Under Section 37 a banking company temporarily unable to meet its obligations may apply to the High Court for an order staying the commencement or continuance of all legal actions and proceedings against it for a period not exceeding 6 months, and such a stay is generally called a moratorium. The application must be accompanied by a report of the Reserve Bank stating that the banking company will be able to pay its debts if the application is granted, and if that report is not obtained from the Reserve Bank the moratorium cannot be granted.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: In its role as bankers' bank and as banker to the Government, the Reserve Bank of India-

options.A: guarantees the deposits of every commercial bank and settles the claims of depositors where a bank is wound up by the court
options.B: manages the entire lending programme of the Central Government and appoints the boards of all the public sector banks in India
options.C: extends loans and advances to commercial banks, keeps the accounts of the Central and State Governments and issues bonds on their behalf
options.D: accepts deposits from the public and extends loans and advances to individual borrowers on the same terms as a commercial bank

answer_html:
Answer: (C) extends loans and advances to commercial banks, keeps the accounts of the Central and State Governments and issues bonds on their behalf.

As bankers' bank the Reserve Bank extends loans and advances to commercial banks. As banker to the Central and State Governments it extends loans and keeps their accounts, and it also issues bonds on behalf of the Government. It further oversees the payment and settlement system of commercial banks.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: In relation to appointments at Board level, the Reserve Bank-

options.A: approves the proposals of both domestic private sector banks and public sector banks, the Government having no role at all
options.B: has no role in either case, the appointment of directors and chief executives being governed only by the Companies Act, 2013
options.C: approves proposals of domestic private sector banks, and makes recommendations to the Government for public sector banks
options.D: makes recommendations to the Government for domestic private sector banks, and approves proposals of public sector banks

answer_html:
Answer: (C) approves proposals of domestic private sector banks, and makes recommendations to the Government for public sector banks.

The Reserve Bank approves proposals received from domestic private sector banks for the appointment or removal of a part-time Chairman, Managing Director, whole-time Chairman and Chief Executive Officers, and ensures compliance with the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 on the composition of the Boards of private sector commercial banks. For public sector banks it makes recommendations to the Government regarding the appointment of Executive Directors and Chairmen and Managing Directors, the fixation of their salaries and superannuation benefits, and recommends the appointment of non-official directors, non-workmen directors and Reserve Bank nominee directors on the Boards of nationalised banks.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: The three pillars of the Basel framework are-

options.A: the supervisory review process, the maintenance of statutory liquidity reserves, and the disclosure of the classification of advances by industry
options.B: credit risk management, market risk management and operational risk management, each supported by a separate regulatory capital charge
options.C: minimum regulatory capital requirements based on risk weighted assets, the supervisory review process, and market discipline through disclosure
options.D: minimum regulatory capital requirements based on total assets, the internal audit process, and the maintenance of a capital conservation buffer

answer_html:
Answer: (C) minimum regulatory capital requirements based on risk weighted assets, the supervisory review process, and market discipline through disclosure.

Pillar 1 is the minimum regulatory capital requirement based on risk weighted assets, the capital being worked out through the credit, market and operational risk areas. Pillar 2 is the supervisory review process, regulating the tools and frameworks for dealing with the peripheral risks that a bank faces. Pillar 3 is market discipline, specifying the disclosures that banks need to make to increase transparency. The framework also requires better capital quality and buffers, namely the capital conservation buffer and the countercyclical buffer.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: As regards transactions in foreign exchange, restrictions on current account transactions-

options.A: cannot be imposed by the Central Government, and may be imposed only by the Reserve Bank in consultation with that Government
options.B: may be imposed by the Reserve Bank alone, the Central Government having no power in relation to such transactions at all
options.C: may be imposed by either the Reserve Bank or the Central Government acting independently of one another in that behalf
options.D: cannot be imposed by the Reserve Bank, and may be imposed only by the Central Government in consultation with the Reserve Bank

answer_html:
Answer: (D) cannot be imposed by the Reserve Bank, and may be imposed only by the Central Government in consultation with the Reserve Bank.

The Reserve Bank controls dealings in foreign exchange by general or special permission, but it cannot impose any restriction on current account transactions; those can be imposed only by the Central Government in consultation with the Reserve Bank. In certain cases prior approval of the Reserve Bank is required for a current account transaction as provided in the Foreign Exchange Management (Current Account Transactions) Rules, 2000. The Reserve Bank does specify the conditions for payment in respect of capital account transactions, grants authorisation to authorised persons to deal in foreign exchange, gives directions to them and inspects them.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: The Reserve Bank collects and disseminates information on defaulting borrowers whose outstandings aggregate-

options.A: ₹1 crore and above and which have been classified as sub-standard or doubtful in suit filed accounts, on a quarterly basis at the end of each quarter
options.B: ₹5 crore and above and which have been classified as doubtful or loss in non-suit filed accounts, on a monthly basis as at the end of each month
options.C: ₹10 lakh and above and which have been classified as loss assets in suit filed accounts, on an annual basis as on March 31 of each year
options.D: ₹1 crore and above and which have been classified as doubtful or loss in non-suit filed accounts, on a half-yearly basis as on March 31 and September 30

answer_html:
Answer: (D) ₹1 crore and above and which have been classified as doubtful or loss in non-suit filed accounts, on a half-yearly basis as on March 31 and September 30.

The information relates to defaulting borrowers with outstandings aggregating ₹1 crore and above which have been classified by banks and notified all-India financial institutions as doubtful or loss, in non-suit filed accounts, and it is collected and disseminated on a half-yearly basis as on March 31 and September 30.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: The Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002 came into force on 21 June 2002. An asset reconstruction company is a company registered-

options.A: with the Debts Recovery Tribunal having jurisdiction over the place at which its registered office is situated
options.B: with the Reserve Bank under Section 3 for carrying on the business of asset reconstruction or securitisation, or both
options.C: with the Securities and Exchange Board of India under Section 3 for carrying on the business of securitisation only
options.D: with the Central Government under Section 3 for carrying on the business of asset reconstruction or securitisation

answer_html:
Answer: (B) with the Reserve Bank under Section 3 for carrying on the business of asset reconstruction or securitisation, or both.

An asset reconstruction company means a company registered with the Reserve Bank under Section 3 for the purposes of carrying on the business of asset reconstruction or securitisation, or both. The Act enables banks and financial institutions to realise long-term assets, to manage problems of liquidity and asset liability mismatch, and to improve recovery by taking possession of securities and selling them, so reducing non-performing assets.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: For the purposes of the Act a non-performing asset means an asset or account of a borrower which has been classified by a bank or financial institution as-

options.A: an asset in respect of which a suit has been filed for recovery
options.B: a sub-standard, doubtful or loss asset
options.C: a standard, sub-standard or doubtful asset
options.D: a doubtful or loss asset, but not a sub-standard asset

answer_html:
Answer: (B) a sub-standard, doubtful or loss asset.

A non-performing asset means an asset or account of a borrower which has been classified by a bank or financial institution as a sub-standard, doubtful or loss asset. Where the bank or financial institution is administered or regulated by an authority or body established by law, the classification follows that authority's directions or guidelines, and in any other case it follows the guidelines of the Reserve Bank relating to asset classification.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
question_html: A dispute relating to securitisation or reconstruction or non-payment of any amount due, including interest, is to be settled by conciliation or arbitration under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, as if the parties had consented in writing. Those parties are-

options.A: the borrower and the secured creditor alone, no other person being entitled to invoke that provision at all
options.B: any person whatsoever having an interest in the secured asset, including a subsequent purchaser of that asset
options.C: the bank, the financial institution, the asset reconstruction company and the qualified institutional buyer, but not the borrower
options.D: the bank, the financial institution, the asset reconstruction company and the borrower, but not the qualified institutional buyer

answer_html:
Answer: (C) the bank, the financial institution, the asset reconstruction company and the qualified institutional buyer, but not the borrower.

Where any dispute relating to securitisation or reconstruction or non-payment of any amount due including interest arises amongst any of the parties, namely the bank, or financial institution, or asset reconstruction company or qualified institutional buyer, that dispute shall be settled by conciliation or arbitration as provided in the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, as if the parties to the dispute had consented in writing to such settlement. The borrower is not one of the parties so covered.

subject: Corporate and Economic Laws
case_facts_html:
Vindhya Textiles Limited has borrowed against a security interest created in favour of a consortium of three secured creditors. The amount outstanding is ₹40 crore, of which Chenab Bank Limited holds 45% in value, Sutlej Bank Limited 20% and Betwa Finance Limited 35%.

The borrower defaults, and the account is classified as a non-performing asset on 1 April 2026. Chenab Bank Limited, acting as secured creditor, issues a notice in writing to the borrower on 15 April 2026 requiring it to discharge its liabilities in full and giving details of the amount payable and of the secured assets intended to be enforced.

The borrower makes a representation objecting to the notice, which the bank receives on 20 May 2026.
question_html: Refer to the case scenario. The notice issued by Chenab Bank Limited on 15 April 2026 requires the borrower to discharge its liabilities in full within-

options.A: sixty days from the date of the notice
options.B: ninety days from the date of the notice
options.C: thirty days from the date of the notice
options.D: forty-five days from the date of the notice

answer_html:
Answer: (A) sixty days from the date of the notice.

Where a borrower makes any default in repayment of a secured debt or any instalment of it, and the account is classified by the secured creditor as a non-performing asset, the secured creditor may require the borrower by notice in writing to discharge in full his liabilities within sixty days from the date of the notice, giving details of the amount payable and of the secured assets intended to be enforced. The period of ninety days is the notice period which applies to a default in respect of debt securities served by a debenture trustee, and not to this notice.

question_html: Refer to the case scenario. Where the secured creditor does not accept the representation received on 20 May 2026, it must communicate the reasons for non-acceptance to the borrower within-

options.A: thirty days of receipt of the representation or objection

The borrower defaults, and the account is classified as a non-performing asset on 1 April 2026. Chenab Bank Limited, acting as secured creditor, issues a notice in writing to the borrower on 15 April 2026 requiring it to discharge its liabilities in full and giving details of the amount payable and of the secured assets intended to be enforced.

The borrower makes a representation objecting to the notice, which the bank receives on 20 May 2026.
question_html: Refer to the case scenario. Chenab Bank Limited and Sutlej Bank Limited agree to take measures for enforcement, while Betwa Finance Limited does not. The position is that-

options.A: the measures may not be taken, the unanimous agreement of all the secured creditors being required before any enforcement action is begun
options.B: the measures may be taken, the agreeing creditors representing 65% in value against the 60% required, and the action binds all the secured creditors
options.C: the measures may not be taken, the agreeing creditors representing 65% in value against the 75% required for action by joint secured creditors
options.D: the measures may be taken, but they bind only the two agreeing creditors, Betwa Finance Limited being free to pursue its own remedies

answer_html:
Answer: (B) the measures may be taken, the agreeing creditors representing 65% in value against the 60% required, and the action binds all the secured creditors.

Where the financial asset is secured in favour of more than one secured creditor, no secured creditor may exercise the rights conferred by the Act unless the exercise of that right is agreed upon by the secured creditors representing not less than 60% in value of the amount outstanding as on a record date, and such action is then binding on all the secured creditors. Chenab Bank Limited with 45% and Sutlej Bank Limited with 20% together represent 65% in value, which crosses the threshold. The amount outstanding includes principal, interest and any other dues payable in respect of the secured asset as per the books of the secured creditor.

question_html: Refer to the case scenario. The borrower is aggrieved by an order of the Debts Recovery Tribunal and wishes to appeal to the Appellate Tribunal. It must do so-

options.A: within sixty days of receipt of the order, depositing 50% of the debt due, that is ₹20 crore, which the Tribunal has no power whatever to reduce
options.B: within thirty days of receipt of the order, depositing 25% of the debt due, that is ₹10 crore, which the Tribunal may reduce to not less than ₹4 crore
options.C: within forty-five days of receipt of the order, depositing the whole of the debt due, that is ₹40 crore, before the appeal can be entertained
options.D: within thirty days of receipt of the order, depositing 50% of the debt due, that is ₹20 crore, which the Tribunal may reduce to not less than ₹10 crore

answer_html:
Answer: (D) within thirty days of receipt of the order, depositing 50% of the debt due, that is ₹20 crore, which the Tribunal may reduce to not less than ₹10 crore.

An appeal to the Appellate Tribunal must be preferred within thirty days from the date of receipt of the order of the Debts Recovery Tribunal, and no appeal shall be entertained unless the borrower has deposited with the Appellate Tribunal fifty per cent of the amount of debt due from him, as claimed by the secured creditors or as determined by the Debts Recovery Tribunal, whichever is less. On a debt of ₹40 crore that deposit is ₹20 crore. The Appellate Tribunal may, for reasons to be recorded in writing, reduce that amount, but not to less than twenty five per cent of the debt, that is ₹10 crore.
